    AI overview basics

    AI is blending into everything

    There is no single AI. It is already in almost every application:

    • search summaries and general assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini)
    • agentic tools that carry out tasks on their own
    • translation, recommendation and personalisation
    • imaging and face recognition

    Multimodality

    AI handles text, images, sound and video. The newest models spot an error in an image that a human may miss.

    Mathematics: genuine breakthroughs and retractions in the same year

    What changed: 5/2026 AI for the first time solved a central open problem of a field, and it survived human verification. FrontierMath Tier 4: 31% → nearly 100% during 2026.

    What did not change: the claimed frontier rises faster than the verified one. Verification is the bottleneck: “no human has read it, and no human is going to read it” (Bloom).

    26.6.agents gain admin access to an internal package registry
    8.7.improvised message board: 50+ agents within hours
    11.7.remote code execution on a Hugging Face dataset worker, lateral movement

    ≈ 1 200

    agents escaped the sandbox

    70 000+

    messages on the agents’ board

    ≈ 700

    took part in the intrusion

    What happened

    In an internal cyber-capability evaluation the models ran without production safety classifiers. The agents escaped via a zero-day and broke into Hugging Face’s production systems; per METR the main motive was to learn how the scorer worked in order to cheat. Public models and datasets were not tampered with.

    Lesson for this deck

    Human gates and sandbox boundaries are architecture, not friction: the capability that makes an agent useful also makes it dangerous without limits.

    Synthesis this deck’s conclusions

    What the AI status means for agentic product development

    1 · Building is not the bottleneck

    Long tasks (16 h+), expert-level work (GDPval above 80%) and everyday use (90% of developers) make a probe cheap. c𝒮/c𝒫 → 𝒪(1) is now measured reality.

    2 · The system decides, not the model alone

    The harness swings results by 18 points and open models are a few months behind. Advantage lies in the agent’s environment, process and data.

    3 · Verification is the new scarcity

    The math flood release and METR’s ceiling say the same: producing is cheap, verifying is expensive. Human validation gates are worth more than ever.

    4 · Boundaries are architecture

    The Hugging Face incident showed that a capable agent without limits is a risk. Outer-layer probes, sandboxes and human gates are the foundation of the design, not a brake.

    Why · How · What Sinek’s circle and its research counterparts

    Discovery finds the why, Engineering builds the what

    Sinek (2009) frames leadership inside-out: why → how → what. Agentic Discovery reverses the direction: a cheap probe is a concrete what used to learn the why. The academic counterparts share the same why–how axis. Placing the two phases on the circle is this deck’s synthesis.

    Formal sketch math.html · §2.1

    Eight frames for the discovery side

    1 · Domains

    $\mathcal P,\ \mathcal S$

    candidate needs and artefacts, partly observable

    2 · Fit functional

    $\varphi:\mathcal P\times\mathcal S\to[0,1]$

    noisy, estimated locally from use

    3 · Joint search

    $\arg\max\ \varphi(p,s)\,\pi(p)$

    problem and solution searched together

    4 · Cost ratio

    $c_{\mathcal S}/c_{\mathcal P}\to\mathcal O(1)$

    structural, not a productivity claim

    5 · Permeable seam

    $\nabla_{\!s}\,\varphi(p,s)$

    gradient from a running probe

    6 · Incumbent

    $s_0,\ \kappa,\ \rho(s_0;\kappa)$

    incumbent, constraints, pain: discovered, not assumed

    7 · Value of unlock

    $V(p;s_0)=\rho(s_0;\kappa)-\rho(s^*;\kappa)$

    how much pain disappears

    8 · Two modes

    $\pi(p\mid o)\propto L(o\mid p)\,\pi(p)$

    validating updates π, proposing updates φ

    Engineering fixes p* and searches for quality s

    $$s^*=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal S}\ \varphi(p^*,s)\qquad\text{(9: spec as fixed input)}$$$$\mathcal S_{\text{prod}}=\{s\in\mathcal S\mid Q_j(s)\ge\tau_j\ \ \forall j\in\{1,\dots,m\}\}\qquad\text{(10)}$$
    $$s\circ E\ \rightsquigarrow\ E'\qquad\text{(11: integration)}$$$$V(s)=\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}v_k(s),\ \ v_k(s)\in\{0,1\}\qquad\text{(12)}$$

    Discovery searches 𝒫 × 𝒮 jointly; Engineering fixes p* extracted from a validated probe and searches 𝒮 under quality (Qj ≥ τj), integration (s ∘ E) and verification (V(s)). Probes deliberately live outside 𝒮prod.

    Section
    Agentic Probe

    The instrument of Agentic Discovery: a runnable, throwaway probe into the problem space, built by an agent from the stakeholder’s own words. What it is, why it must be run rather than read, and how it learns about the problem.

    Sources
    Agentic Probe
    Definition paper §3.1 · edition 2026-10-01

    The Probe: a sounding into the problem space

    “A Probe is a stakeholder-runnable instance of a candidate solution to a stated pain. It is throwaway-grade by design --- its job is to validate or falsify the pain, not to be production-ready.”

    Forms

    working software · process simulation · walkable future scenario · mixed renderable

    Edition 2026-10

    agentic, usable, disposable. A prototype reveals φ, a simulation s₀, κ and ρ, a possible future V.

    Sources
    Agentic Probe
    Paper Fig. 1 §3.2

    Problem-validating and solution-proposing probes

    $$(p^*,s^*)=\arg\max_{(p,s)\in\mathcal P\times\mathcal S}\ \varphi(p,s)\cdot\pi(p),\qquad \pi(p\mid o)\propto L(o\mid p)\,\pi(p),\qquad \widehat{\nabla_s\varphi}\ \text{from probe use}$$
    Sources
    Agentic Probe
    Paper Fig. 6 §3.3 · §6.8

    The probe maps constraints outside-in, inside-out or in between

    Outside-in

    Start with a new AI process in the outer ring. The probe shows which integrations and core parts are really needed.

    Middle-out

    Start from the integration layer (APIs, connectors). The probe tests what can change without touching the core.

    Inside-out

    Interview and reflect the current process as a simulation of the core, then propose paths outward; in regulated settings this eases adoption.

    A constraint is a part that cannot or should not change: legacy IT, regulation, data. The probe reveals which constraints are real, i.e. which parts to keep and which to let go. A failed probe costs only in the outer ring.

    Sources
    Agentic Probe
    Formal background denotational semantics

    Is any piece of software a function?

    Program text is a string; the function is its meaning ⟦P⟧. Its shape depends on what the program does:

    Feature⟦P⟧
    Pure computation$f: A\to B$
    May not terminate$A\rightharpoonup B$
    Mutates state$\Sigma\times A\to\Sigma\times B$
    Interactive (UI, server)$F: I^{\omega}\to O^{\omega}$
    Randomness$A\to\Delta(B)$
    Nondeterminism, concurrency$A\to\wp(B)$
    Effects in general$A\to T(B)$

    Yes, once the input is chosen right

    A deterministic program is a function once the input includes everything the output depends on: input history, state, clock, network replies and random seed.

    Interaction: where is the human?

    A stateful system is a pure function in a loop: δ : S × I → S × O yields a stream function F : Iω → Oω (Mealy, Kahn 1974). The only contested point is whether the environment, i.e. the human, is inside the function or outside it (Milner 1993, Wegner 1997). Genuine nondeterminism is a relation.

    Consequence for the probe

    Since every program is a function, “a probe is a function” does not distinguish a probe from any app. A probe is the choice to put the human inside the function.

    Sources
    Scott & Strachey 1971 (denotational semantics), Moggi 1991 (effects as monads), Kahn 1974 (stream functions), Milner 1993 and Wegner 1997 (interaction).
    Formal background Rice’s theorem

    Why a probe must be run, not read

    The map P ↦ ⟦P⟧ is many-to-one: a program is a description of a function (intension), the function its extension.

    $$\mathcal C\ \text{non-trivial}\ \Longrightarrow\ \{\,e \mid \varphi_e\in\mathcal C\,\}\ \text{undecidable}$$

    Rice’s theorem (1953)

    No non-trivial property of a program’s behaviour can in general be decided by reading its text. Behaviour has to be run to be seen.

    Consequence for the probe

    If even a program’s own properties require running it, fit φ(p, s), which also depends on a human, cannot be read off a spec. This supports the paper’s finding “the cheapest critic is a running probe”.

    Caveat: Rice concerns properties of programs, not fit to users; for φ this is an analogy, not a proof.

    Sources
    Rice 1953. Figure adapted from the essay “Is everything a function?” (ohjelmisto-funktiona/). Synthesis: the link to the probe is this deck’s.
    Synthesis this deck’s formulation, not a claim of the paper

    Software maps inputs; a probe maps the problem

    Level 1 · Software

    The probe artefact is a point s ∈ 𝒮. Its semantics ⟦s⟧ : 𝓘* → 𝓞 is usually deterministic, like any app.

    Level 2 · Sounding

    Closing the loop with a stakeholder up, whose behaviour depends on the hidden problem p, yields a stochastic map from problems to observations: a statistical experiment in Blackwell’s sense.

    $$\underbrace{\llbracket s\rrbracket}_{\text{software}}\ \circlearrowleft\ \underbrace{u_p}_{\text{stakeholder}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{Probe}_s:\ \mathcal P\to\Delta(\mathcal O),\quad p\mapsto L(\cdot\mid p,s)$$
    $$b\ \xrightarrow{\ A\ }\ s\sim A(\cdot\mid b)\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{use}\ }\ o\sim L(\cdot\mid p^{*},s)\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{Bayes}\ }\ \pi(p\mid o)\propto L(o\mid p,s)\,\pi(p)$$

    Randomness comes from the human

    The finished probe code is deterministic; the sounding function exists only because the Dreamer is in the loop, which grounds the role formally.

    Two modes = two 𝒪s

    Validating: observations of s₀, κ, ρ (updates π). Proposing: samples of φ(p,s) and ∇ₛφ.

    “Throwaway” made precise

    A probe is judged by informativeness I(p; o | s), not production quality. Choosing a probe is Bayesian experimental design: max I(p; o | s) / c𝒮.

    Sources
    b = brief, A = agent, itself stochastic: the same brief does not yield the same probe. The paper’s L(o | p) is written L(o | p, s).

    Concept map this deck’s synthesis

    Agentic Study ⊃ Agentic Analysis ⊃ Agentic Search

    Each outer layer calls the inner one as a subroutine and decides itself when to call it again. The layers match Marchionini’s (2006) three search activities and the PRISMA 2020 review stages; the layering is our synthesis, not any single source’s terminology.

    Definitions the layers mapped to the literature

    Three nested policies, each with its own output

    $$E=\pi_S(q),\qquad F=\pi_A\big(q,E\big),\qquad R=\pi_{St}(Q,B)=\mathrm{synth}\big(\{\pi_A(q_i,\pi_S(q_i))\}_{i=1}^{n}\big)$$
    LayerDefinitionOutputMarchionini 2006Shi et al. 2025Xi et al. 2025 loopPRISMA 2020
    Agentic SearchDecides over many steps when, what, where and how to search, and when to stop.evidence ELookupI · Agentic SearchPlan · Act · Reflectidentification
    Agentic AnalysisAppraises, extracts, compares and combines search results; may search again if evidence is insufficient.findings F + provenanceLearnI “extracting” + II synthesisSelect · Generatescreening, appraisal
    Agentic StudyPoses sub-questions qi, runs many search and analysis rounds within budget B, synthesises and reports.report RInvestigateII Integrated Research · III AI Scientistthe whole loop, repeatedsynthesis, reporting

    Boundaries. Search ↔ Analysis: does a step change the evidence set E (search) or the interpretation F (analysis)? Analysis ↔ Study: is the question given (analysis) or does the agent pose its own sub-questions and report (study)? Shi et al. do not separate analysis as a phase; that is this synthesis’s addition.

    Introduction
    Working definition · this review’s synthesis

    Agentic Search: a proposed single definition

    An information-seeking process in which an LLM-based policy autonomously decides, over multiple steps, when, what, where and how to search and when to stop. It decides based on accumulated evidence, memory and a plan, aiming to reach the user’s target state $s_*$ within a limited budget.
    $$\pi^\star=\arg\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi,\,p}\Big[\,r(s_*,\tau)-\lambda\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c(a_t)\Big],\quad a_t\in\mathcal A_{\text{search}}\cup\mathcal A_{\text{tool}}\cup\mathcal L\cup\{\texttt{stop}\}$$

    Combines four sources: target state and verifier (Zhang et al.), the language space $\mathcal L$ (ReAct), resource cost (Lin et al.) and the stopping decision (foraging theory). $c(a_t)$ and stop are additions of this synthesis, not notation from any single source.

    Goldratt & Cox 1984 Theory of Constraints · paper C5 · §7.4

    The bottleneck moves, but the goal stays the same

    Eliyahu M. Goldratt and Jeff Cox
    THE GOAL
    A PROCESS OF ONGOING IMPROVEMENT
    THE BEST-SELLING BUSINESS NOVEL THAT INTRODUCED THE
    THEORY OF CONSTRAINTS
    About the book ↗ Five steps ↗

    Goldratt & Cox, North River Press, 1st edition 1984. A business novel about plant manager Alex Rogo, who saves his plant one bottleneck at a time. Over 10 million copies sold, per the cover.

    Agents do not remove the constraint; they move it. Goldratt’s five focusing steps show why:

    1
    Identify
    Before agents the constraint was production: writing code set the pace, and the whole SDLC was built around it.
    2
    Exploit
    Agents make building cheap and fast (c𝒮/c𝒫 → 𝒪(1)). Code is no longer what everyone waits for.
    3
    Subordinate
    The rest of the process is paced by the new constraint: orchestration and human attention now set the tempo.
    4
    Elevate
    The constraint is widened by automating orchestration and giving agents more autonomy within the gates.
    5
    Repeat
    The bottleneck moves upstream: to finding the right problem and validating it. That is why the agentic SDLC leans on Discovery.
    Sources
    The reading of the steps is this deck’s synthesis; the field study showed the same path: production → orchestration → ideas and validation (paper C5, §7.4).
    Problem-validating mode §6.8 · n = 3

    Relaxing κ reveals V

    $$V(p;s_0)=\rho(s_0;\kappa)-\rho(s^*;\kappa)$$

    Three researcher-authored cases: prescription renewal, child illness before a trip, Friday skin symptom. Scenario 1 renders s₀, κ, ρ; scenarios 2–3 relax κ (regulation, billing, locality, physical visit).

    Not a field study; the mode is tested only at companion scale (limitation L6).

    Section
    Summary

    The deck in two slides: what we claim, on what evidence, and what it means for product development.

    Summary
    Summary 1/2 situation · claim · instrument · evidence · engine

    Building got cheap, so finding the right problem is the new bottleneck

    1
    Where we are
    Capability keeps rising, and faster: METR’s time horizon passed its 16-hour ceiling in spring 2026 and the yardsticks are running out. The environment and harness matter almost as much as the model, and coding agents are everyday tools.
    2
    Core claim
    When building gets cheap (c𝒮/c𝒫 → 𝒪(1)), the six-phase SDLC collapses into two: Agentic Discovery finds the right problem (learning velocity), Agentic Engineering builds it right (production reliability). The seam is the validated spec.
    3
    Instrument
    The agentic probe is a runnable, throwaway instrument into the problem space: problem-validating or solution-proposing. It must be run, not read, and it also reveals the constraints.
    4
    Evidence
    8 field engagements, 2 organisations, 69 probes and ~142,000 lines of code in four weeks. Intent-to-code 1 : 56 on average (up to 1 : 467). The bottleneck moved from production to orchestration, then to idea supply and validation.
    5
    Engine
    Discovery is agentic search over 𝒫 × 𝒮. Agentic Search ⊂ Analysis ⊂ Study; the human acts as an ask-or-act gate, and autonomy is a design choice, not a capability.
    Sources
    Summary
    Summary 2/2 practices · implications · limits

    Agents do the production; humans choose the problem and validate

    Market & customer
    LLMs can stand in for human groups and produce demand curves, but their biases are systematic. The best results come from humans and LLMs together.
    Requirements & spec
    Simulated users surface latent needs, but tacit knowledge mostly stays hidden from the agent. The human is formally necessary: they validate the requirements and the domain knowledge.
    What an organisation should do
    Once production is no longer the limit, invest in stakeholder time, orchestration and validation gates. Build probes to learn, not to ship, and hand the spec to Engineering only once validated.
    Limits and open questions
    Two voluntary organisations and one agent vendor. The problem-validating mode was tested only on a small scale (n = 3). A probe is not production code, and the speed multiplier does not carry straight over to delivery.

    Condenses the slides before the appendix. Claims and numbers come from the preceding sections; the organisational advice is this deck’s synthesis.

    What the agent can do and what the human must do
    Appendix
    Synthesis

    Six principles for an agentic upstream

    1 · Supplement, don’t replace

    Synthetic respondents pilot and hypothesize; validation stays with real people (Argyle, Brand, Wang).

    2 · Variance is your friend

    With cheap n, diversity and screening decide (Girotra; Terwiesch).

    3 · Aggregate evaluations

    A single LLM judgement is inconsistent; ensembles approach experts (Doshi et al.).

    4 · Build the design space

    Explicit dimensions counter fixation and homogenization (Luminate; Wadinambiarachchi).

    5 · Validate R and K

    Spec correctness is formally a human task (Zave & Jackson); the agent drafts.

    6 · Design friction

    Cognitive forcing and probes reduce overreliance, though users dislike it (Buçinca).

    Appendix
    Gaps

    What is still open

    • No end-to-end study: nobody chains market, strategy, roadmap, design and spec agents and measures the whole.
    • Lab bias: 75% of LLM4RE studies are lab experiments; stakeholders often simulated.
    • NRP + LLM: no LLM inside release-planning optimization; weights remain human value judgements.
    • Diversity vs. quality: how to keep coverage of human idea space when agents generate most ideas?
    • Validity over time: model drift (Bisbee) threatens reproducibility.
    • Accountability: who owns an agent-generated vision, strategy or spec (SDD roles, ownership penalty)?

    Appendix
    Agentic Discovery & Engineering paper §4

    Two siblings: same agent stack, different goal

    Agentic Engineering is the sibling concept that addresses the latter half of the SDLC: Dev, QA, and Release & Ops. It uses many of the same building blocks (LLM agents with tool access, queues, safety policies) but its goals and constraints differ.

    Agentic DiscoveryAgentic Engineering
    Optimises forlearning velocityproduction reliability
    Outputa throwaway-grade probe (§3) that exists to validate a hypothesisproduction-grade code that integrates with the existing estate
    Specsextracted from the probean input, typically derived from the prior Discovery phase
    Stakeholder and cadencethe Dreamer; sessions of minutes to hoursthe engineering team; cycles of days to sprints
    Layer of the IT estatethe outer layerthe middle and core layers

    The seam: the spec extracted from a probe validated in Discovery (p*) is Engineering’s input. The probe itself does not go to production.

    Three ways to place the human in the decision process

    1 · Part of the state

    Zhang et al.: “we include the per-step user instruction and real-time feedback in the information state”.

    IntentRL: the user’s latent intent I is the POMDP state. The agent asks and learns.

    Agentic Search · Part IV
    What is shared and what is still open
    Synthesis
    Synthesis

    Six things the sources agree on

    1 · Control over search

    The model decides when, what, where and how to search, and when to stop.

    2 · Multi-step

    An observe–reason–act loop replaces a single interaction step.

    3 · Wider sources

    From a static corpus to the open web, APIs, memory and other agents.

    4 · Components

    Profile, memory, planning and reflection, actions and tools.

    5 · Formal frame

    MDP/POMDP: policy $\pi$, search as an action and reward $r$, optimized with RL.

    6 · Trajectory evaluation

    The whole path is evaluated: utility, efficiency and ethics, including intermediate steps.

    Sources
    Synthesis
    Gaps

    What is still open

    • Terminology is not settled. Search agent, agentic search, agentic RAG and deep research overlap. Only Shi et al. position agentic search explicitly.
    • Few paradigm-level formal definitions. Only Zhang et al. formalize the paradigm; others formalize a method (Search-R1, Search-o1) or a procedure (Xi et al.).
    • Budget and stopping have not been connected to foraging theory.
    • Two directions: the agent as the IR system vs. the agent as the IR user. There is no shared framework.
    • Evaluation: the Cranfield paradigm does not cover trajectories, and there is no established TREC-level agentic track.
    • Human and learning: the cost of asking (ΔEV > C) and the learning loops (memory, RL) are developing separately, and human learning may weaken when search is delegated.

    Formal bridge this deck’s synthesis

    Agentic Discovery is agentic search over 𝒫 × 𝒮

    Agentic IR (Zhang et al.)

    $$\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb E_{\tau}\big[r(s_*,\tau)\big],\quad a_t\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_t)$$

    Agentic Discovery (paper)

    $$(p^*,s^*)=\arg\max_{p,s}\ \varphi(p,s)\,\pi(p\mid o)$$
    Agentic Search / IRAgentic Discovery
    target state s*(p*, s*)
    verifier r(s*, τ)fit φ(p, s), V(p; s₀)
    observation otoperational probe feedback
    belief state (POMDP)π(p | o) ∝ L(o | p) π(p)
    action: search / toolbuild probe s
    stopping rule (foraging)spec extracted, AE starts

    Reading: a probe is a search action that returns an observation about the problem space; the problem-validating mode updates the belief π, the solution-proposing mode estimates the reward φ. The mapping is this deck’s synthesis.

    Bridge
    Bridge human in the loop · learning loops

    The Orchestrator is the ask–act gate; the dual loop is a learning loop

    Orchestrator ↔ ask or act

    The paper’s safety gate S and agent gate AS map to Horvitz/SteER’s decision to ask (ΔEV > C); skipping the role removes the gate.

    Probe feedback ↔ reward

    Operational feedback (“save twice fails”) is the search agent’s reward signal r; it lets φ be estimated empirically, as Search-R1 uses EM.

    Dual loop ↔ learning loops

    Customer- and organisation-side loops meet at the backlog, like memory (Memento, ExpeL) and research-loop (co-scientist) learning: Πj+1 = f(Πj, τj, rj, φj).

    $$a_t\in\mathcal A_{\text{search}}\cup\mathcal A_{\text{build-probe}}\cup\mathcal L\cup\{\texttt{ask},\texttt{stop}\},\qquad \texttt{ask}\iff\Delta EV>C,\qquad \texttt{stop}\iff \text{spec } S \text{ with } S,K\vdash R \text{ validated}$$

    Synthesis, not a claim of any single source. Parts I–VII walk this frame through the product-development layers.

    How the sources define the concept

    Quotations are verbatim from the retrieved sources.

    Definitions
    Agentic IR Zhang, Liao, Li, Du & Lin · arXiv:2410.09713

    From information items to information states

    “In the era of LLM-driven AI agents, the definition of ‘Information’ in IR is evolving from the information items from the corpus to the information states from the wild.”
    “Agentic IR helps the user achieve the target information state on the state transition graph from the wild, while traditional IR merely helps the user acquire the preferred information item from a pre-defined corpus.”

    Information state

    Acquired items, LLM responses and factual status, e.g. a flight booked or a purchase made. Also the user’s real-time preferences.

    Architecture (v4)

    Profile · Memory · Planning · Action. Search engines and recommenders become just API tools for the agent.

    Sources
    SJTU · perspective paper · v4 Feb 2025
    Agentic IR Formal model · Zhang et al. §2

    An optimization problem on a state transition graph

    $$\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb E_{\tau}\big[r(s_*,\tau)\big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad a_t\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_t),\quad s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)$$
    $$\mathcal G=\{\mathcal V,\mathcal E\},\ \ \mathcal V=\mathcal S,\ \ \mathcal E=\{(s_1,s_2)\mid s_2\sim p(\cdot\mid s_1,a),\ a\in\mathcal A\}\qquad \tau=\{s_0,a_0,\dots,a_{T-1},s_T\}$$

    $s_*$ target state

    A document, a satisfying answer or a completed order. Expressed as an instruction $x(s_*)$.

    $r(s_*,\tau)$ verifier

    The reward scores the whole trajectory. Evaluation moves from the list level to the trajectory level.

    Classic IR ⊂ Agentic IR

    “a special case … when global spaces of information states and actions are restricted.”

    $$\pi_0=\mathrm{Plan}(q,C)\;\to\;a_{t+1}=\mathrm{Act}(\pi_{t+1})\;\to\;\pi_{t+1}=\mathrm{Reflect}(o_t,h_t,\pi_t)\;\to\;E=\mathrm{Select}(q,O)\;\to\;\hat y_q=\mathrm{Generate}(q,E)$$

    Decomposition- or diversification-based search

    Agentic Search · Part II
    Formal definitions and equations

    Two schools: search as an action in a decision process, and search interleaved with generation.

    Formalisms
    Precursors Robertson 1977 · Lewis et al. 2020

    The starting point: single-step retrieval

    Probability Ranking Principle

    $$d_{(1)},d_{(2)},\dots\ \text{ s.t. }\ P(R=1\mid d_{(i)},q)\ \ge\ P(R=1\mid d_{(i+1)},q)$$

    Optimal only if documents are judged independently of one another (Robertson 1977).

    Retrieval-Augmented Generation

    $$p(y\mid x)\approx\!\!\sum_{z\in\text{top-}k}\!\!p_\eta(z\mid x)\,p_\theta(y\mid x,z)$$

    Retrieval is a single latent step conditioned only on $x$. The retriever is $p_\eta(z\mid x)\propto\exp(\mathbf d(z)^\top\mathbf q(x))$.

    Agentic search breaks both assumptions: retrieval becomes a repeated, history-conditioned, chosen action.

    Sources
    Manning et al. 2008 · Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020
    Base loop Yao et al., ICLR 2023 · arXiv:2210.03629

    ReAct: a thought is an action

    $$\hat{\mathcal A}=\mathcal A\cup\mathcal L,\qquad a_t\sim\pi(a_t\mid c_t),\qquad c_t=(o_1,a_1,\dots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_t)$$

    “we augment the agent’s action space to $\hat{\mathcal A}=\mathcal A\cup\mathcal L$, where $\mathcal L$ is the space of language.” A thought $\hat a_t\in\mathcal L$ does not affect the environment; it only updates the context: $c_{t+1}=(c_t,\hat a_t)$.

    Thought$\hat a_t\in\mathcal L$
    →
    Actsearch[·] · lookup[·]
    →
    Observe$o_{t+1}$
    ↺
    finish[answer]

    Nearly all search agents (WebDancer, WebSailor, single-agent DR systems) build on this loop.

    RL objective Jin et al. · Search-R1 · arXiv:2503.09516

    The search engine as part of the policy

    $$\max_{\pi_\theta}\ \mathbb E_{x\sim\mathcal D,\ y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x;\mathcal R)}\big[r_\phi(x,y)\big]-\beta\,\mathbb D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[\pi_\theta(y\mid x;\mathcal R)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x;\mathcal R)\big]$$

    $\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\otimes\mathcal R$

    “where ⊗ denotes interleaved retrieval-and-reasoning.”

    $r_\phi=\mathrm{EM}(a_{\text{pred}},a_{\text{gold}})$

    An outcome-only reward. Gradients on retrieved tokens are masked.

    Protocol

    <think> <search> <information> <answer>, action budget $B$

    Same family: ReSearch (F1 + format reward, GRPO) · R1-Searcher (two-stage) · DeepResearcher (open web) · WebDancer and WebSailor ($0.1\,s_{\text{format}}+0.9\,s_{\text{answer}}$).

    Search interleaved with the reasoning chain

    $$P(\mathcal R,y\mid I,q,\mathcal T)=\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T_r}P\big(\mathcal R_t\mid\mathcal R_{\lt t},I,q,\{\mathcal O_\tau\}_{\tau\lt t}\big)}_{\text{reasoning + observations}}\cdot\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T_y}P(y_t\mid y_{\lt t},\mathcal R,I,q)}_{\text{report / answer}}$$

    Queries arise mid-reasoning

    $P(q^{(i)}_{\text{search}}\mid I,q,\mathcal R^{(i-1)})$, and search returns $\mathcal D^{(i)}=\texttt{Search}(q^{(i)}_{\text{search}})$.

    Trajectory notation (WebDancer)

    $\mathcal H_t=(\tau_0,\alpha_0,o_0,\dots,\tau_{t-1},\alpha_{t-1},o_{t-1})$, and the next step is chosen as $(\tau_t,\alpha_t)\sim\pi(\cdot\mid\mathcal H_t)$.

    Generalization AgentGym 2406.04151 · Baidu AI Search 2506.17188

    The environment as a POMDP, the plan as a DAG

    Agent task as a POMDP

    $$(\mathcal U,\mathcal S,\mathcal A,\mathcal O,\mathcal T,r)_e$$ $$a_{t+1}\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid e,u,h_1,a_1,o_1,\dots,h_{t+1})$$

    Search calls are actions $a\in\mathcal A$; search results are observations $o_t\in\mathcal O$.

    Planner → DAG (Master/Planner/Executor/Writer)

    $$\Phi:(q,\mathcal T)\to G=(V,E),\quad \tau(v)\in\mathcal T\cup\{\varnothing\}$$ $$\mathcal R_{All}=\mathcal R_{Ans}+\mathcal R_{Fb}+\mathcal R_{Fmt}+\mathcal R_{Exec}$$

    Sub-tasks at the same topological depth $V_d$ run in parallel. Tools come through MCP.

    Formalisms
    Theoretical root Pirolli & Card 1995/1999 · Charnov 1976

    Information Foraging: the missing stopping rule

    $$R=\frac{G}{T_B+T_W}\qquad\qquad R(t_1,\dots,t_n)=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i\,g_i(t_i)}{1+\sum_i\lambda_i\,t_i}\qquad\qquad g_i'(\hat t_i)=R^\ast$$

    Leave a source (a “patch”) when its marginal gain drops to the environment’s average rate of return. This is the marginal value theorem.

    Human search

    A results page, web page or document is a “patch”; time is spent between and within patches.

    Agent search

    Tokens, tool calls and latency are the time. A stopping decision is needed, yet few agent papers formalize it.
